title: A Chef's Meditation on Feeding Strangers Well
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Twenty years behind a stove taught me that hospitality collapses the instant it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat.
Narrator: I've fed critics who reviewed me harshly and fed strangers who wandered in penniless, and I've tried, imperfectly, to plate both meals with identical attention.
Narrator: [carefully] Tried, I say, because the temptation to punish a bad review with a mediocre second dish is considerably stronger than any cookbook ever admits openly.
Narrator: I've indulged that temptation exactly once, early in my career, and the resulting dish tasted precisely as resentful as I felt while plating it.
Narrator: [reflective] Adab in a kitchen, I've come to think, isn't primarily about technique, however much technique dominates the actual training we receive.
Narrator: It's about extending the same unhurried attention to the guest who can't afford dessert as to the one settling a considerable bill without glancing at it twice.
Narrator: [honestly] My grandmother, who ran a considerably humbler kitchen than mine, used to say a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income.
Narrator: I didn't understand that as instruction until years into my own career, plating food for people whose worth I'd begun, quietly, ranking by their tips alone.
Narrator: [gently] Ranking guests, I eventually noticed, is a peculiar kind of theft, taking something that was never mine to withhold selectively in the first place.
Narrator: The example set toward guests in our tradition was never calibrated to their status, and I've spent considerable effort since trying, imperfectly, to plate accordingly.
Narrator: [calmly] Some nights the kitchen is chaos, tickets stacking faster than we can manage, and generosity becomes the first casualty of that particular chaos.
Narrator: On those nights I try hardest, not because generosity comes easily under pressure, but precisely because it doesn't, and that's rather when it counts most.
Narrator: [encouraging] Every plate that leaves my kitchen, I hope, carries less of my judgment about who deserves it and more of whatever hospitality actually requires of me.

quiz.question: What did twenty years behind a stove teach the narrator about hospitality?
options: That hospitality collapses the instant it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat
That hospitality should focus on wealthy guests only
That hospitality is unrelated to how food is served
That hospitality only matters for critics
quiz.explanation: He learned hospitality collapses the moment it starts calculating who deserves the good cuts of meat.

quiz.question: What happened the one time the narrator gave in to the temptation to punish a bad reviewer?
options: The dish turned out perfectly regardless
The resulting dish tasted precisely as resentful as he felt while plating it
He was praised for his honesty
Nothing different happened at all
quiz.explanation: He indulged the temptation once and the dish tasted precisely as resentful as he felt while making it.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandmother used to say about a guest's hunger?
options: That it only matters for paying customers
That hunger should be ignored during busy nights
That a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income
That only regular customers deserve full attention
quiz.explanation: His grandmother said a guest's hunger doesn't announce itself according to their income.

quiz.question: What does the narrator call the practice of ranking guests by their tips?
options: A necessary business practice
An acceptable part of running a restaurant
Something his grandmother taught him to do
A peculiar kind of theft, taking something that was never his to withhold selectively
quiz.explanation: He calls ranking guests a peculiar kind of theft, taking something never his to withhold selectively.

quiz.question: When does the narrator say he tries hardest to be generous?
options: On chaotic nights, precisely because generosity doesn't come easily under pressure
Only on slow, calm nights
Only when critics are present
He says generosity never varies by circumstance
quiz.explanation: He tries hardest on chaotic nights, because generosity doesn't come easily under pressure, which is when it counts most.

quiz.question: What does the chef identify as the core of adab in a kitchen?
options: Perfect technique regardless of how guests are treated
Giving guests unhurried attention regardless of perceived status
Serving only critics who have been kind to the restaurant
Using higher prices to identify deserving diners
quiz.explanation: The chef frames hospitality as equal attention for guests who differ in money, status, and treatment of the restaurant.

quiz.question: Which past failure supports the chef's self-critique?
options: He refused to serve a critic who had reviewed him harshly
He charged a stranger extra for dessert
He once plated a resentful dish after receiving a bad review
He dismissed his grandmother's advice as impractical
quiz.explanation: He admits one resentful response to a bad review and uses the bad dish as evidence that resentment shaped his care.

quiz.question: What qualification does the chef make about generosity under pressure?
options: Generosity matters only when service is calm
A busy kitchen excuses selective attention to guests
Pressure proves that hospitality is unrealistic
Generosity is hardest in chaos, which makes practicing it more important
quiz.explanation: The chef recognises that pressure makes generosity difficult, and therefore treats those moments as its real test.

quiz.question: Which stance does the chef take toward judging guests by status?
options: He treats it as a personal failure he must resist
He sees it as necessary for a profitable restaurant
He considers it harmless when customers leave large tips
He believes guests should explain their income before ordering
quiz.explanation: He calls ranking guests a kind of theft and describes trying to remove his own judgment from each plate.

quiz.question: What implication follows from the chef's account of hospitality?
options: Hospitality is mainly a reward for respectful guests
Care must be sustained especially when pressure invites selective treatment
A chef should conceal dissatisfaction with every customer
Technical training removes the need for moral discipline
quiz.explanation: The narration makes pressure the setting in which equal care is most difficult and most meaningful.
